<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{Main} 
All closed geodesics in an arithmetic complex hyperbolic surface of second type are simple.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
For every arithmetic complex hyperbolic surface $M$, precisely one of the following holds: 
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]
$M$ has infinitely many non-simple closed geodesics (in which case $M$ is of first type), or
\item[(ii)]
$M$ has only simple closed geodesics (in which case $M$ is of second type).
\end{itemize}
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
${\rm Isom}^0({\rm H}_\mathbb{C}^n)={\rm PU}(n,1)$, and ${\rm Isom}({\rm H}_\mathbb{C}^n)={\rm PU}(n,1) \ltimes \mathbb{Z}/2$ (adjoining a real reflection, see below).
\medskip
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{conjclasses} 
\quad
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] 
Any elliptic element is semisimple, with eigenvalues of norm 1. Two elliptic elements are conjugate in ${\rm U}(n,1)$ if and only if they have the same eigenvalues and the same eigenvalue of negative type.
\item[(b)] 
Any loxodromic element is semisimple, with exactly $n-1$ eigenvalues of norm 1. Two loxodromic elements are conjugate in ${\rm U}(n,1)$ if and only if they have the same eigenvalues.
\item[(c)] 
Any parabolic element is not semisimple, and all its eigenvalues have norm 1. It has a unique decomposition $g=pe=ep$ with $p$ unipotent and $e$ elliptic. Two parabolic elements are conjugate in ${\rm U}(n,1)$ if and only if their unipotent and elliptic components are conjugate.
\item[(d)] 
There are two classes of unipotent elements for $n>1$, the vertical Heisenberg translations and the non-vertical Heisenberg translations.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
A {\em complex $k$--plane} is a projective $k$--dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{C} P^n$ intersecting $\pi(V^-)$ non-trivially (so, it is an isometrically embedded copy of ${\rm H}_\mathbb{C}^{k} \subset {\rm H}_\mathbb{C}^n$). Complex 1--planes are usually called {\em complex lines}. A {\em complex reflection} is an elliptic isometry $g\in {\rm PU}(n,1)$ whose fixed-point set is a complex $(n-1)$--plane.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{invX} 
Let $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$ be 4 distinct points in $\partial_\infty {\rm H}_\mathbb{C}^n$.
\begin{itemize}
\item For $g \in {\rm PU}(n,1)$, we have ${\bf X}(g(p_1),g(p_2),g(p_3),g(p_4))={\bf X}(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)$ . 
\item If $g$ is an antiholomorphic isometry, then ${\bf X}(g(p_1),g(p_2),g(p_3),g(p_4))=\overline{{\bf X}(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)}$. 
\end{itemize}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
Let $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$ be 4 distinct points in $\partial_\infty {\rm H}_\mathbb{C}^n$. Then:
\begin{itemize}
\item ${\bf X}(p_2,p_1,p_4,p_3)={\bf X}(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)$
\item ${\bf X}(p_3,p_4,p_1,p_2)=\overline{{\bf X}(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)}$
\item ${\bf X}(p_2,p_1,p_3,p_4)={\bf X}(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)^{-1}$
\end{itemize}
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{IrrationalAngle} 
If $\Gamma$ is an arithmetic lattice of second type in ${\rm SU}(2,1)$ and $\gamma \in \Gamma$ is loxodromic, then the holonomy of $\gamma$ has infinite order.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{RealTrace} 
Let $A,B,C \in {\rm SU}(2,1)$ with $B=C^{-1}AC$ such that $A$ and $B$ are loxodromic isometries with intersecting axes. Then ${\rm Tr} \, A^{-1}B$ is real; in particular, if $ A^{-1}B$ is loxodromic, then its holonomy is $\pm 1$.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- rmk-1: body_md -->
In the case of real hyperbolic 3--space studied by Chinburg and Reid, the intersecting axes must lie in a totally geodesic plane, forcing the four endpoints to have a real cross-ratio. They then use this to show that ${\rm Tr} \, [A,B^{-1}] \in \mathbb{R}$. The situation here is different:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] The intersecting axes generically do not lie in a totally geodesic subspace. Indeed, given any three distinct points $p_1,p_2,p_3 \in \partial_\infty {\rm H}^2_\mathbb{C}$, there exists $p_4 \in \partial_\infty {\rm H}^2_\mathbb{C}$ such that the geodesics $(p_1, p_2)$ and $(p_3, p_4)$ intersect: just take $p_4 = g(p_3)$, where $g$ is the central involution centered at any point of $(p_1, p_2)$.
\item[(b)] In fact, here the condition ${\rm Tr} \, [A,B^{-1}] \in \mathbb{R}$ will only be satisfied when the four points $p_A,q_A,p_B,q_B$ lie on the boundary of a totally geodesic real plane in ${\rm H}_\mathbb{C}^2$. Indeed, by the main result of \cite{W}, if ${\rm Tr} [A,B^{-1}] \in \mathbb{R}$ then there exists a real reflection $\sigma$ exchanging $p_A$ and $q_A$ as well as $p_B$ and $q_B$. But then $\sigma g$ would be an antiholomorphic isometry fixing these four points, which can only happen if  the four points lie on the boundary of a totally geodesic real plane.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end rmk-1 -->
<!-- rmk-2: body_md -->
The conclusion of Theorem~\ref{RealTrace} does not hold if ${\rm SU}(2,1)$ is replaced by ${\rm PSL}(2,\mathbb{C})$, even when $A$ and $B$ are chosen within a cocompact lattice in ${\rm PSL}(2,\mathbb{C}) \cong {\rm Isom}^+({\rm H}_\mathbb{R}^3)$. Indeed, let $K \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a complex cubic field, and $\mathcal{O}_K$ be the ring of integers of $K$. Then $\Gamma:= {\rm SO}(3,\mathcal{O}_K)$ is a cocompact arithmetic lattice in ${\rm SO}(3,\mathbb{C}) \cong {\rm PSL}(2,\mathbb{C})$ and every loxodromic element of $\Gamma$ has infinite-order holonomy (equivalently, there is no infinite-order element of $\Gamma$ all of whose eigenvalues are real); see Theorem~5.3.1 in~\cite{MR}. On the other hand, the two diagonal matrices ${\rm diag}(1, -1, -1), {\rm diag}(-1,-1,1) \in \Gamma$ are conjugate within $\Gamma$ (indeed, within ${\rm SO}(3,\mathbb{Z})$), and so their centralizers within~$\Gamma$, which are each virtually infinite cyclic, are also conjugate within~$\Gamma$. If $A$ is a sufficiently high power of a loxodromic element of $\Gamma$ centralizing ${\rm diag}(1, -1, -1)$, and $B$ is an element of~$\Gamma$ conjugate to $A$ in $\Gamma$ and centralizing ${\rm diag}(-1,-1,1)$, then $A^{-1}B$ is loxodromic and, like all other loxodromic elements of $\Gamma$, has infinite-order holonomy. However, the axis of $A$ in ${\rm H}_\mathbb{R}^3$ intersects that of $B$; indeed, the axis of $A$ (respectively, the axis of $B$) is the fixed-point set of ${\rm diag}(1, -1, -1)$ (resp., of ${\rm diag}(-1,-1,1)$), and these fixed-point sets intersect, as can be seen from the fact that $AB$ again has finite order.
<!-- end rmk-2 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{NonSimpleHolonomy} 
Assume $M={\rm H}^2_\mathbb{C}/\Gamma$ is a compact manifold; that is, $\Gamma \simeq \pi_1(M)$ is a torsion-free cocompact lattice in ${\rm PU}(2,1)$. If $M$ contains a non-simple closed geodesic, then $\Gamma$ contains a loxodromic element with trivial holonomy.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
